strings.mistakes_d_doubt_p1: If this is the first time, or losing count is not a regular occurrence for you, the prayer is void: stop and begin it again. If it happens to you often, act on whichever judgement you find strongest; and if you have none, build on the smaller number you are sure of, sitting at each point that might be the end of the prayer.
strings.mistakes_d_doubt_p1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — Doubt During Prayer
strings.mistakes_d_doubt_p2: Assume you have not done it. Build on the smaller number, finish the prayer, and prostrate before the salams.
strings.mistakes_d_doubt_p3: Build on what you are certain of and pray the raka’ah you are unsure about, then prostrate after the salam.
strings.mistakes_d_doubt_p4: Proceed on what you are certain of — the smaller number. An imam instead acts on what he judges more likely, and prostrates after the salam.
strings.mistakes_d_doubt_p4_src: Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 6: The Two Prostrations of Forgetfulness
strings.mistakes_d_doubt_subject: What to do when you lose count.
strings.mistakes_d_extra_p1: If you have not yet prostrated in the extra raka’ah, return to the sitting and prostrate for forgetfulness. If you have already prostrated in it and had not made the final sitting, the obligatory prayer turns into a voluntary one — and the obligatory prayer must then be prayed again.
strings.mistakes_d_extra_p1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Prostrations of Forgetfulness
strings.mistakes_d_extra_p2: Adding an action absentmindedly does not invalidate the prayer, though adding it deliberately would. Prostrate for forgetfulness.
strings.mistakes_d_extra_p2_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f9.6, f11.1
strings.mistakes_d_extra_p3: Prostrate after the salam, this being an addition. Adding a great deal — four raka’at to a four-raka’ah prayer — invalidates it instead.
strings.mistakes_d_extra_p4: Sit down the moment you realise, and prostrate. Adding an action deliberately would invalidate the prayer; absentmindedly, it calls for the prostration.
strings.mistakes_d_extra_p4_src: Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 6: The Two Prostrations of Forgetfulness
strings.mistakes_d_fatiha_p1: The pillar is reciting Qur’an; the Fatiha in particular is wajib. Leaving it out forgetfully calls for sujood as-sahw.
strings.mistakes_d_fatiha_p1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Pillars Of Prayer, and The Wajib Elements Of Prayer
strings.mistakes_d_fatiha_p2: The Fatiha is one of the prayer’s seventeen integrals.
strings.mistakes_d_fatiha_p3: On the approved position the raka’ah it was left out of is invalid, and another raka’ah replaces it.
strings.mistakes_d_fatiha_p4: Reciting the Fatiha, in Arabic, is a pillar; dropping a pillar invalidates the prayer.
strings.mistakes_d_fatiha_p4_src: Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 5: The Pillars of Prayer and Its Mandatory and Recommended Acts
strings.mistakes_d_settling_p1: Coming to rest a moment in each pillar is wajib. Leaving it out forgetfully calls for sujood as-sahw rather than invalidating the prayer.
strings.mistakes_d_settling_p1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Wajib Elements Of Prayer
strings.mistakes_d_settling_p2: Settling is an integral in four places: in bowing, on straightening up, in prostration, and sitting between the prostrations. Without them the raka’ah is not performed.
strings.mistakes_d_settling_p3: The text fixes only the shortest prostration — the time the body takes to come fully to rest. Its commentary adds that this stillness is obligatory in every pillar, not prostration alone.
strings.mistakes_d_settling_p3_src: The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 10.1, “Length of prostration”
strings.mistakes_d_settling_p4: Tranquility in all of the pillars is itself listed among the twelve pillars of the prayer.
strings.mistakes_d_settling_p4_src: Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 5: The Pillars of Prayer and Its Mandatory and Recommended Acts
strings.mistakes_d_speech_p1: Speech voids the prayer even when it is forgetful or a slip of the tongue. Sujood as-sahw does not repair it; the prayer is prayed again.
strings.mistakes_d_speech_p1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — Nullifications of Prayer
strings.mistakes_d_speech_p2: A slight amount, where there is an excuse — speaking absentmindedly, or being new to Islam and not knowing it was forbidden — does not invalidate the prayer, and calls for the prostration. Much speech, meaning more than about six words, invalidates it even with an excuse.
strings.mistakes_d_speech_p2_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f9.1, f11.6
strings.mistakes_d_speech_p3: A little speech, while you have forgotten you are praying, calls for the two prostrations after the salam. Deliberate speech invalidates the prayer; the commentary makes an exception for words that serve no purpose, and even those invalidate it if they are many.
strings.mistakes_d_speech_p4: This guide does not state a Hanbali position here. The manual it was checked against is an abridgement with no chapter on what invalidates the prayer, and guessing would be worse than saying so. Ask someone who teaches this school.
strings.mistakes_d_tashahhud_p1: Sit back down if you are not yet fully standing. Once you are fully up, carry on and prostrate for forgetfulness at the end rather than go back — but going back does not ruin the prayer, on the soundest report. Returning when you were nearer standing than sitting also calls for the prostration.
strings.mistakes_d_tashahhud_p1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Prostrations of Forgetfulness
strings.mistakes_d_tashahhud_p2: Once you have stood it is unlawful to go back, and going back deliberately invalidates the prayer. If you return absentmindedly or not knowing, stand again as soon as you remember and prostrate for it. If you check yourself before standing and sit down again, nothing is owed.
strings.mistakes_d_tashahhud_p3: The first tashahhud, and the sitting for it, are confirmed sunnas: leaving them out calls for the two prostrations before the salam.
strings.mistakes_d_tashahhud_p4: Go back and perform it if you remember before you are fully upright. Once fully upright, do not go back.
strings.mistakes_d_tashahhud_p4_src: Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 6: The Two Prostrations of Forgetfulness
strings.mistakes_d_timing_p1: After the salam. Say the salam to the right, make the two prostrations, then the tashahhud, the blessings on the Prophet ﷺ and du’a, and finish with the salams. Making them before the salam is somewhat disliked.
strings.mistakes_d_timing_p1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — When To Perform The Prostrations Of Forgetfulness
strings.mistakes_d_timing_p2: Before the final salams, whether the cause was something added or something left out.
strings.mistakes_d_timing_p3: Before the salam for something left out; after the salam for something added; and before the salam when both happened in the same prayer.
strings.mistakes_d_timing_p4: Before the salam in every case but three: someone who gave the salam before the prayer was complete, an imam who acted on what he judged more likely, and someone who forgot to prostrate before the salam. Those three prostrate after the salam, then make the tashahhud and the salam.
strings.mistakes_d_timing_p4_src: Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 6: The Two Prostrations of Forgetfulness
strings.mistakes_d_trigger_p1: Forgetfully leaving out a wajib (necessary) act of the prayer. The two prostrations are then required — and required only once, however many acts were left out.
strings.mistakes_d_trigger_p1_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Prostrations of Forgetfulness
strings.mistakes_d_trigger_p2: Two causes: leaving out one of the prayer’s six main sunnas, or doing something the prayer does not call for. The prostration itself is a sunna, not an obligation.
strings.mistakes_d_trigger_p2_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f11.1, f11.12
strings.mistakes_d_trigger_p3: Adding something inadvertently; leaving out one of the eight confirmed sunnas; or leaving out two slight sunnas together. Leaving out only one slight sunna calls for nothing.
strings.mistakes_d_trigger_p4: Three kinds of lapse: an addition, leaving out a mandatory act, or doubt.
strings.mistakes_d_trigger_p4_src: Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 6: The Two Prostrations of Forgetfulness
strings.mistakes_editions: Each school’s position is cited to a manual of that school: Reliance of the Traveller for Shafi’i, Nur al-Idah for Hanafi, The Risala for Maliki, Umdat al-Fiqh for Hanbali. Section numbers follow the English editions listed here.
strings.mistakes_intro: Everyone makes mistakes in prayer. Most are repaired by two extra prostrations called sujood as-sahw. Some need nothing at all. A few mean the prayer has to be prayed again — and no prostration changes that. This guide sorts them, and gives each school’s position where they differ.
strings.mistakes_s1_body: Sujood as-sahw — “the prostration of forgetfulness” — is two prostrations added to the prayer because something in it went wrong. They are the same prostration you already make in every raka’ah; the name only says why you are making them.
strings.mistakes_s1_count: However many mistakes were made in a single prayer, it is still two prostrations — not two for each.
strings.mistakes_s1_count_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f11.10; The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 12.2b
strings.mistakes_s1_limit: It repairs a defect. It does not stand in for a part of the prayer that was never performed, and it cannot rescue a prayer that has already become invalid. Those are the last two sections of this guide.
strings.mistakes_s2_body: This is the difference you are most likely to notice in a mosque, because the person praying beside you may do it at a different moment than you do. All four schools make two prostrations. They place them differently.
strings.mistakes_s2_heading: Before the salam, or after it
strings.mistakes_s2_imam: Praying behind an imam, follow the imam. The schools agree that his forgetfulness binds those behind him, whatever their own school would have them do alone.
strings.mistakes_s2_imam_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f11.11; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Prostrations of Forgetfulness; The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 11.6a; Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 6: The Two Prostrations of Forgetfulness
strings.mistakes_s3_body: The prostrations themselves are made exactly as the prostrations inside the prayer. When they fall — and what still follows them — differs by school, and is covered in the section above.
strings.mistakes_s3_down1_detail: The same prostration you make in every raka’ah.
strings.mistakes_s3_down2_title: Say “Allahu akbar” and prostrate a second time.
strings.mistakes_s3_finish_detail: What happens from here differs by school: see “Before the salam, or after it” above.
strings.mistakes_s3_finish_title: Sit up and complete the prayer.
strings.mistakes_s3_sit_detail: As you sit between the two prostrations of a raka’ah.
strings.mistakes_s4_1_detail: The most common of all, and the one on which the schools are furthest apart — one of them has you start the prayer again.
strings.mistakes_s4_1_title: You do not know whether you have prayed three raka’at or four
strings.mistakes_s4_2_title: You forgot the first tashahhud and started to stand
strings.mistakes_s4_3_title: You realise you have prayed a raka’ah too many
strings.mistakes_s4_body: Four cases that come up constantly. Each is one where the schools reach genuinely different answers, so the position shown for your own school is the one to act on.
strings.mistakes_s4_heading: Situations you are likely to meet
strings.mistakes_s5_body: Not every slip needs repairing. Each school draws the line in its own place, and all of them leave a great deal outside it.
strings.mistakes_s5_hanafi: Hanafi: leaving out a sunna of the prayer, even on purpose, neither invalidates the prayer nor calls for the prostration — though leaving one out on purpose is still blameworthy.
strings.mistakes_s5_hanafi_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Sunan of Prayer
strings.mistakes_s5_hanbali: Hanbali: the merely preferable acts. Leaving them out neither invalidates the prayer nor makes the prostration due.
strings.mistakes_s5_hanbali_src: Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 5: The Pillars of Prayer and Its Mandatory and Recommended Acts
strings.mistakes_s5_maliki: Maliki: leaving out only a slight sunna. Once a long time has passed, nothing is owed for it at all.
strings.mistakes_s5_shafii: Shafi’i: turning the head, or taking a step or two; scratching yourself, or staying silent a long time; anything that is neither an integral of the prayer nor one of the six main sunnas; or merely suspecting — without actually believing — that you did something calling for the prostration.
strings.mistakes_s5_shafii_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f9.8, f11.4, f11.5, f11.9
strings.mistakes_s6_awrah_detail: Putting it right immediately does not invalidate the prayer.
strings.mistakes_s6_awrah_title: Uncovering the awrah, or filth reaching your clothes, and not putting it right at once
strings.mistakes_s6_body: These are not defects to be repaired. The prayer has ended, or never validly began. It is prayed again, and two prostrations do not change that.
strings.mistakes_s6_deliberate_detail: In the Hanafi school this is a sin and the prayer is repeated. In the Hanbali manual used here, leaving out a mandatory act on purpose invalidates the prayer.
strings.mistakes_s6_deliberate_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — Intentionally Omitting A Necessary [Wajib] Act; Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 5: The Pillars of Prayer and Its Mandatory and Recommended Acts
strings.mistakes_s6_deliberate_title: Deliberately leaving out something your school holds obligatory
strings.mistakes_s6_eat_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f9.5; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — Nullifications of Prayer
strings.mistakes_s6_integral_detail: Among them: the intention, the opening takbir, standing, the Fatiha, bowing, prostrating, coming to rest in each, the final tashahhud, the salam. These are the prayer itself; a prostration does not stand in for one.
strings.mistakes_s6_integral_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f9.14; The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 12.2k, 12.2l
strings.mistakes_s6_integral_title: Leaving out an integral of the prayer and never making it up
strings.mistakes_s6_note: If you realise the prayer was invalid, pray it again. That is not a failure — it is the correction the law itself provides.
strings.mistakes_s6_qibla_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — Nullifications of Prayer
strings.mistakes_s6_qibla_title: Turning the chest away from the qibla with no reason for it
strings.mistakes_s6_speech_detail: Three consecutive steps, or three consecutive movements, count as much.
strings.mistakes_s6_speech_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f9.1, f9.7; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — Nullifications of Prayer
strings.mistakes_s6_speech_title: Much speech, or much continuous movement
strings.mistakes_s6_wudu_detail: Even absentmindedly. Purity is a condition of the prayer, not a part of it.
strings.mistakes_s7_1_detail: Coming up from bowing and going straight down; lifting the head from prostration and moving on before the joints have come to rest. A man prayed this way in front of the Prophet ﷺ, who sent him back three times with “Go back and pray, for you have not prayed”, then taught him to come to rest in each position.
strings.mistakes_s7_1_src: Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 5: The Pillars of Prayer and Its Mandatory and Recommended Acts; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Wajib Elements Of Prayer
strings.mistakes_s7_1_title: Rushing — not letting the body settle
strings.mistakes_s7_body: These come up constantly, and most of them are avoided simply by knowing they exist.
strings.mistakes_s7_imam_detail: Finishing one integral before he reaches it is unlawful, though the prayer stands. Finishing two ahead of him deliberately invalidates the prayer; doing so absentmindedly costs you the raka’ah.
strings.mistakes_s7_repeat_detail: Repeating out of misgiving feeds the misgiving. Guard against it.
strings.mistakes_s7_repeat_src: Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — Branches, p. 240
strings.mistakes_s7_repeat_title: Praying it again because you doubt the first one was good enough
strings.mistakes_s7_time_detail: Knowing, or believing, that the time has entered is one of the prayer’s eight conditions.
strings.mistakes_s7_time_title: Praying before the time has come in
strings.mistakes_s7_waswasa_detail: A nagging, ever-present sense that you have slipped up somewhere is not to be acted on. Let it pass and carry on; taking it seriously only feeds it.
strings.mistakes_s7_which_detail: Believing some parts are obligatory and some merely recommended, while not knowing which are which, invalidates the prayer. Believing all of it obligatory does not. This is a reason to learn the difference rather than a reason to worry.
strings.mistakes_s7_which_title: Not knowing which parts of the prayer are obligatory
strings.mistakes_s8_agree_1: The prostration of forgetfulness is two prostrations — never more, however many mistakes were made.
strings.mistakes_s8_agree_2: Leaving out a pillar of the prayer is not repaired by prostrating for it.
strings.mistakes_s8_agree_3: An imam’s forgetfulness is followed by those praying behind him.
strings.mistakes_s8_agree_src: Reliance of the Traveller, f11.2, f11.10, f11.11; Nur al-Idah, Book ii: Prayer — The Prostrations of Forgetfulness; The Risala (Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani), 11.6a, 12.2b, 12.2k; Umdat al-Fiqh (Ibn Qudamah), Book 2 ch. 6: The Two Prostrations of Forgetfulness
strings.mistakes_s8_body: Under all the differences above, all four schools hold that:
strings.mistakes_s8_differ: They differ on the points marked in this guide: what makes the prostration due and how binding it is, whether it falls before or after the salam, what to do when you lose count, forgetting the first tashahhud, an extra raka’ah, speaking by accident, rushing, and the standing of the Fatiha.
strings.mistakes_src_nur: Nur al-Idah, Hasan al-Shurunbulali — Hanafi. Book ii (Prayer) was read directly for this guide.
strings.mistakes_src_reliance: Reliance of the Traveller (Umdat al-Salik), Ahmad ibn Naqib al-Misri, tr. Nuh Ha Mim Keller — Shafi’i. Book f was read directly for this guide.
strings.mistakes_src_risala: The Risala, Ibn Abi Zayd al-Qayrawani, tr. Bello Mohammad Daura, with the commentary of al-Azhari — Maliki. Chapters 10 and 12 were read directly for this guide.
strings.mistakes_src_umdah: Umdat al-Fiqh, Ibn Qudamah al-Maqdisi, translated with commentary by Hatem al-Haj — Hanbali. Book 2, chapters 5 and 6 were read directly for this guide.
strings.mistakes_summary: Sujood as-sahw, and what to do when something goes wrong
strings.mistakes_unreviewed: No qualified scholar has checked this guide. Every ruling in it was checked against a manual of the school it is credited to, and names where — but that verifies the transcription, not the fiqh. Treat this as a draft and ask someone qualified before you rely on it.
